hypothesis.title: payment CPU limit reduced to 50m causes saturation and throttling
hypothesis.summary: A configuration change 16 minutes before the alert reduced payment's CPU limit from 500m to 50m. Payment immediately hit 96-100% CPU utilization with 88% throttling, causing its p95 latency to spike from 44ms to 1903ms. Payment began timing out with "deadline exceeded" errors, which propagated upstream to checkout, triggering the CheckoutLatencyHigh alert. The workload remained stable; only the resource constraint changed.
hypothesis.reasoning: The alert fired on checkout latency, but the evidence clearly points upstream to payment. Traces show payment spans account for +1900ms of added latency, and 83% of failing checkout traces end in payment with "deadline exceeded" errors. Payment's p95 latency spiked from ~44ms to ~1903ms at -10m, matching the checkout latency spike. Payment CPU utilization jumped from ~12% to 96-100% at the same time, with a CPUThrottlingHigh event showing 88% throttling. The critical clue is the config change 16m before the alert: payment's CPU limit was reduced from 500m to 50m. This is a 10× reduction in available CPU. Payment's request rate remained stable (~3 req/s), so the workload didn't change—only the available resources did. The product-catalog deploy at -38m is a red herring: it happened well before symptoms started, and product-catalog's own metrics show no issues. The frontend-proxy restart (exit 137, likely OOMKilled) is unrelated—frontend-proxy is not on the failing trace path and has no evidence of causing checkout issues. This matches postmortem PM-2026-04-22 (ad CPU saturation) where a CPU limit + throttling caused latency and deadline errors.

supporting_evidence.why_it_matters: Payment CPU limit was reduced from 500m to 50m exactly 16 minutes before the alert, a 10× reduction that directly caused the resource constraint.
Payment CPU jumped from 12% to 96-100% at -10m, coinciding with the latency spike and confirming CPU saturation after the limit change.
88% CPU throttling on payment container confirms the service is being heavily throttled by the new 50m limit, directly causing slowdowns.
Payment p95 latency spiked from 44ms to 1903ms at -10m, showing the service became 40× slower after hitting the CPU limit.
Failing trace shows payment span taking 1750ms and ending in 'deadline exceeded', proving payment is the origin of checkout failures.
83 ERROR logs in payment with 'deadline exceeded' starting at -15m confirm payment is timing out under CPU pressure.

suggested_actions.title: Revert payment CPU limit to 500m
suggested_actions.rationale: Restores the previous working CPU limit. This is the safest and most direct mitigation since the 50m limit is clearly insufficient for the current workload.

suggested_actions.title: Scale payment horizontally to 3 replicas
suggested_actions.rationale: Distributes load across more pods to reduce per-pod CPU pressure while keeping the 50m limit. Useful if the limit change was intentional for cost reasons.

suggested_actions.title: Monitor payment CPU and latency recovery
suggested_actions.rationale: Verify that CPU utilization drops below 80% and p95 latency returns to baseline (~44ms) after mitigation.

alternatives.why_less_likely: Product-catalog deployed version 2.0.3 at -38m, but payment symptoms (CPU spike, latency) only started at -10m, 28 minutes later. Product-catalog is not on the failing trace path (checkout → payment), and there is no evidence of product-catalog degradation in the telemetry.

retrieved_documents.title: CPU saturation and throttling
retrieved_documents.snippet: 1. `kubectl -n otel-demo top pod -l app.kubernetes.io/name=<svc>` - at the limit? 2. Was the CPU limit changed recently? `kubectl -n otel-demo get deploy <svc> -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].resources}'` 3. Mitigate: scale out (`kubectl scale`) or raise the limit (`kubectl set resources`).
